claim: The superior colliculus (SC) is an evolutionary conserved structure located in the midbrain.
source: One of the most studied biological models to investigate the formation and function of sensory connectivity -or sensory maps- from both experimental and theoretical standpoints is the superior colliculus (SC), an evolutionary conserved structure located in the midbrain (Cang and Feldheim, 2013; Basso and May, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cang and Feldheim, 2013 and Basso and May, 2017

claim: In most vertebrates, the SC is the premier brain center for integrating sensory inputs from visual, auditory and somatosensory modalities distributed in different interacting laminae.
source: In most vertebrates, the SC is the premier brain center for integrating sensory inputs from visual, auditory and somatosensory modalities distributed in different interacting laminae.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about the SC

claim: The SC is a key node in the network of brain areas responsible for controlling the location of attention and even decision-making.
source: This structure is a key node in the network of brain areas responsible for controlling the location of attention and even decision-making (Basso and May, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Basso and May, 2017

claim: Visual inputs in the superficial layers of the SC correspond to the organized projections from the retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) in the retina (the retino-collicular (RC) projections) and from layer V neurons in the primary visual cortex V1 (the cortico-collicular [CC] projections).
source: Visual inputs in the superficial layers of the SC correspond to the organized projections from the retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) in the retina (the retino-collicular (RC) projections) and from layer V neurons in the primary visual cortex V1 (the cortico-collicular [CC] projections).
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about SC anatomy

claim: Both RC and CC projections form visual maps that must be aligned and in register to allow efficient detection of visual stimuli.
source: Both projections form visual maps that must be aligned and in register to allow efficient detection of visual stimuli (Basso and May, 2017; Liang et al., 2015; Zhao et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Basso and May, 2017; Liang et al., 2015; Zhao et al., 2014

claim: The formation of the RC map involves gradients of Eph tyrosine kinases receptors (Eph) and their cognate membrane-bound ligands, the ephrins (Efn), together with competition between axons for collicular space and correlated neuronal activity in the form of spontaneous waves.
source: Previous studies on RC mapping have revealed the involvement of gradients of Eph tyrosine kinases receptors (Eph) and their cognate membrane-bound ligands, the ephrins (Efn), together with competition between axons for collicular space and correlated neuronal activity in the form of spontaneous waves (Ackman and Crair, 2014; Cang and Feldheim, 2013; Triplett et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ackman and Crair, 2014; Cang and Feldheim, 2013; Triplett et al., 2011

claim: The formation of the RC map occurs prior to the establishment of the CC map.
source: Interestingly, the formation of the RC map occurs prior to the establishment of the CC map.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge

claim: The existence of the RC map is necessary for the formation of the CC map, suggesting an interdependence of the two mechanisms.
source: Other studies have shown that the existence of the RC map is necessary for the formation of the CC map, suggesting an interdependence of the two mechanisms (Khachab and Bruce, 1999; Rhoades et al., 1985; Triplett et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Khachab and Bruce, 1999; Rhoades et al., 1985; Triplett et al., 2009

claim: In Isl2-Epha3KI mutants, the Epha3 receptor is ectopically expressed in 50% of RGCs, leading to a duplication of the RC map.
source: Another piece of evidence came from the study of map alignment in the Isl2-Epha3KI, one of the best characterized mutant in the field. In these mutants, the Epha3 receptor is ectopically expressed in 50% of RGCs, leading to a duplication of the RC map (Brown et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brown et al., 2000

claim: A full duplication of the CC map is observed in the Isl2Epha3/Epha3 homozygous mutants, which display a normal retinotopy in the visual cortex.
source: Strikingly, a full duplication of the CC map is also observed in the Isl2Epha3/Epha3 homozygous mutants, which display a normal retinotopy in the visual cortex (Triplett et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Triplett et al., 2009

claim: The Isl2-Efna3KI mutant over-expresses the ligand Efna3 in 50% of the RGCs.
source: To gain insight into the implication of molecular guidance cues in the retina in the alignment of visual maps in the SC, we have characterized a new mutant, the Isl2-Efna3KI, which over-expresses the ligand Efna3 in 50% of the RGCs (Savier et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Savier et al., 2017

claim: The Isl2-Efna3KI mutant does not display any defect in the formation of the RC map, however the subsequent CC map is duplicated.
source: To our surprise, this mutant does not display any defect in the formation of the RC map, however the subsequent CC map is duplicated.
evidence: Draws from experimental observations described in the manuscript

claim: The Koulakov model was the most faithful among tested models for reproducing experimental findings.
source: Recently, Hjorth et al., 2015 developed a pipeline which allowed for systematic testing of the currently available models and revealed that most cannot reproduce all nuances of experimental findings (Isl2-Epha3KI, EfnaKOs and Math5KO). Among those tested, the most faithful was the Koulakov model, which had recently been extended to explain the variability in the phenotypes observed in a particular mouse model, the Isl2-Epha3KI (Owens et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hjorth et al., 2015 and Owens et al., 2015

claim: The 3-step map alignment model simulates the formation of the RC map and, for the first time, the subsequent formation and alignment of the CC map along the rostral-caudal axis of the SC.
source: The 3-step map alignment model simulates the formation of the RC map and, for the first time, the subsequent formation and alignment of the CC map along the rostral-caudal axis of the SC based on experimental and mechanistic evidence (Savier et al., 2017; Savier and Reber, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Savier et al., 2017 and Savier and Reber, 2018

claim: The 3-step map alignment algorithm predicts normal wild-type (WT) mapping as well as the map alignment defects observed in the Isl2-Efna3KI animals.
source: This algorithm predicts normal wild-type (WT) mapping as well as the map alignment defects observed in the Isl2-Efna3KI animals (Savier et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Savier et al., 2017

claim: The 3-step map alignment algorithm accurately simulates both RC and CC mapping defects in Isl2-Epha3KI mutants.
source: Here we demonstrate that the 3-step map alignment algorithm accurately simulates both RC and CC mapping defects in Isl2-Epha3KI mutants (Brown et al., 2000; Triplett et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in the manuscript and citations to Brown et al., 2000 and Triplett et al., 2009

claim: Ectopic expression of Epha3 in Isl2(+) RGCs does not affect retinal Efna co-expression.
source: However, whether EPHA3 ectopic expression in Isl2-positive (Isl2(+)) RGCs affects retinal Efna co-expression is unknown. We performed a quantitative analysis of retinal Efna transcripts in P1/P2 nasal, central, and temporal acutely isolated RGCs (Savier et al., 2017), revealing similar expression levels between Isl2Epha3/Epha3 and WT littermates.
evidence: Supported by experimental qPCR data presented in Figure 1A

claim: The graded expression of Efna2 and Efna5 running from high-nasal to low-temporal is preserved in Isl2Epha3/Epha3 animals.
source: The graded expression of Efna2 and Efna5 running form high-nasal to low-temporal is preserved in Isl2Epha3/Epha3 animals, whereas the expression of Efna3 as well as Epha3 is homogeneous (Figure 1A – Figure 1—source data 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: The expression of Efna3 as well as Epha3 is homogeneous in Isl2Epha3/Epha3 animals.
source: The graded expression of Efna2 and Efna5 running form high-nasal to low-temporal is preserved in Isl2Epha3/Epha3 animals, whereas the expression of Efna3 as well as Epha3 is homogeneous (Figure 1A – Figure 1—source data 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: Transcript analyses in V1 and SC revealed similar levels of Efna2/a3/a5 and Epha4/a7 receptors in Isl2Epha3/Epha3 compared to WT littermates at P7.
source: Transcript analyses in V1 and SC (Figure 1B – Figure 1—source data 1B) revealed similar levels of Efna2/a3/a5 and Epha4/a7 receptors in Isl2Epha3/Epha3 compared to WT littermates at P7 excluding indirect effects on mapping due to local changes of Ephas/Efnas gene expression.
evidence: Supported by experimental qPCR data shown in Figure 1B

claim: The equations modeling retinal, collicular and cortical Efna gradients as well as cortical Epha gradients related to the Isl2-Epha3KI genotypes are equivalent to the equations previously characterized in WT animals.
source: We can reasonably assume that the equations modeling retinal, collicular and cortical Efna gradients as well as cortical Epha gradients related to the Isl2-Epha3KI genotypes are equivalent to the equations previously characterized (measured experimentally or estimated) in WT animals (Reber et al., 2004; Cang et al., 2005; Tsigankov and Koulakov, 2006; Tsigankov and Koulakov, 2010; Bevins et al., 2011; Savier et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data and supported by multiple citations

claim: The 3-step map alignment model simulates a continuous, single RC map for WT animals.
source: Results showed a continuous, single map for WT (Figure 2E), as expected from previous experimental findings and theoretical modeling (Brown et al., 2000; Reber et al., 2004; Savier et al., 2017; Bevins et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2E and citations to previous work

claim: For the Isl2Epha3/+, partially duplicated RC mapping is modeled, together with the presence of a collapse point for temporal-most RGCs.
source: For the Isl2Epha3/+, partially duplicated RC mapping is modeled, together with the presence of a collapse point for temporal-most RGCs (Figure 2K) as extensively observed experimentally (Brown et al., 2000; Reber et al., 2004; Bevins et al., 2011) and theoretically (Reber et al., 2004; Willshaw, 2006; Tsigankov and Koulakov, 2010; Simpson and Goodhill, 2011).
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2K and citations to experimental and theoretical work

claim: For Isl2Epha3/Epha3, the RC map is fully duplicated.
source: For Isl2Epha3/Epha3, the RC map is fully duplicated, similarly to previous experimental and theoretical findings (Figure 2Q; Brown et al., 2000; Reber et al., 2004; Willshaw, 2006; Tsigankov and Koulakov, 2010; Bevins et al., 2011; Simpson and Goodhill, 2011).
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2Q and citations to previous work

claim: For WT, the transposition of retinal Efna gradients to the SC generates a smooth monotonically increasing gradient.
source: For WT, this generates a smooth monotonically increasing gradient (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2C

claim: For the Isl2Epha3/+ genotype, the transposition of retinal Efna gradients generates a double oscillatory gradient of retinal Efnas in the SC.
source: For the Isl2Epha3/+ genotype, this transposition generates a double oscillatory gradient of retinal Efnas in the SC (Figure 2I), a consequence of the partial duplication of the RC map (Figure 2K).
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2I and inference from the RC map duplication

claim: For the Isl2Epha3/Epha3, the transposition of the retinal Efna gradients, according to the fully duplicated RC map, generated a double oscillatory gradient of transposed retinal Efnas in the SC.
source: For the Isl2Epha3/Epha3, the transposition of the retinal Efna gradients, according to the fully duplicated RC map (Figure 2Q), generated a double oscillatory gradient of transposed retinal Efnas in the SC (Figure 2O).
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2O and inference from the RC map duplication

claim: The WT CC map is smooth and continuous.
source: The WT CC map is smooth and continuous (Figure 2F), similarly to the RC map (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2F

claim: The Isl2Epha3/+ simulations show dispersed projections forming two separated maps collapsing in the rostral-most part of the SC from lateral-most V1 neurons.
source: The Isl2Epha3/+ simulations show dispersed projections forming two separated maps collapsing in the rostral-most part of the SC from lateral-most V1 neurons (Figure 2L).
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2L

claim: CC map simulations for the Isl2Epha3/Epha3 genotype show dispersed projections forming two fully separated maps.
source: CC map simulations for the Isl2Epha3/Epha3 genotype shows dispersed projections forming two fully separated maps (Figure 2R).
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2R

claim: In Isl2Epha3/+ animals, experimental measurements match with the theoretical representation of the RC map.
source: Our experimental measurements (triangles and square, Figure 3B – Figure 3—source data 1B) match with the theoretical representation (black dots, black/gray lines Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by comparison of experimental and simulated data shown in Figure 3B

claim: CC anterograde tracing in Isl2Epha3/+ animals revealed a partially duplicated CC map with the occurrence of a collapse point near 82% of the medial-lateral axis of V1 (16% of the rostral-caudal axis of the SC).
source: CC anterograde tracing (Figure 3D, n = 15, red dots/lines – Figure 3—source data 1D), performed as described earlier (Savier et al., 2017), revealed a partially duplicated CC map with the occurrence of a collapse point near 82% of the medial-lateral axis of V1 (16% of the rostral-caudal axis of the SC), similarly to the simulated map (black dots, black/gray lines Figure 3D, two-samples Kolmogorov-Smirnov test).
evidence: Supported by experimental tracing data shown in Figure 3D and statistical comparison with simulated map

claim: In Isl2Epha3/Epha3, experimental RC duplications match with the simulated mapping.
source: In Isl2Epha3/Epha3, RC duplications are observed as shown by two experimental measurements (triangles and squares) plotted on the RC map (Figure 3E,F – Figure 3—source data 1F) and as extensively described previously (Brown et al., 2000; Reber et al., 2004). These experimental data match with the simulated mapping (black dots, black/gray lines Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by comparison of experimental and simulated data shown in Figure 3F and citations to previous work

claim: CC map tracing in vivo in Isl2Epha3/Epha3 revealed a fully duplicated CC map, as predicted by the simulations.
source: CC map tracing in vivo (Figure 3G,H, red dots/line, n = 7 – Figure 3—source data 1H) revealed a fully duplicated CC map, as predicted by the simulations (Figure 3H, black dots, black/gray lines, two-samples Kolmogorov-Smirnov test).
evidence: Supported by experimental tracing data shown in Figure 3H and statistical comparison with simulated map

claim: In WT animals, median IDIretino = 5.66, 95% CI [5.15; 6.17], median IDIcortico = 8.12 [7.63; 8.60] and median AI = 2.23 [2.13; 2.33].
source: In WT animals, median IDIretino = 5.66, 95% CI [5.15; 6.17], median IDIcortico = 8.12 [7.63; 8.60] and median AI = 2.23 [2.13; 2.33] (Figure 4A,G – Figure 4—source data 1A, G).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 4A,G

claim: In Isl2Epha3/+, median IDIretino = 38.8 [36.8; 40.8], median IDIcortico = 38.0 [36.1; 40.0] and median AI = 2.07 [1.95; 2.19].
source: In Isl2Epha3/+, median IDIretino = 38.8 [36.8; 40.8], median IDIcortico = 38.0 [36.1; 40.0] and median AI = 2.07 [1.95; 2.19] (Figure 4A – Figure 4—source data 1A) indicating increased spreading of both RC and CC projections, due to the partially duplicated maps (Figure 4C, black and white dots).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 4A and inference from map duplication

claim: The median AI value in Isl2Epha3/+ is not statistically different from WT, suggesting that Isl2Epha3/+ RC/CC maps are aligned.
source: The median AI value in Isl2Epha3/+ (2.07 [1.95, 2.19]) is not statistically different from WT (Figure 4G – Figure 4—source data 1G), suggesting that Isl2Epha3/+ RC/CC maps are aligned (Figure 4C, black and white dots).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4G and inference from AI values

claim: In the Isl2Epha3/Epha3 animals, median IDIretino = 51.7 [50.8; 52.6], median IDIcortico = 50.6 [49.7; 51.5] and median AI = 2.2 [2.08; 2.32].
source: In the Isl2Epha3/Epha3 animals, median IDIretino = 51.7 [50.8; 52.6], median IDIcortico = 50.6 [49.7; 51.5] and median AI = 2.2 [2.08; 2.32] (Figure 4A,G - Figure 4—source data 1A,G), indicating an increased separation between the RCand CC maps compared to WT and Isl2Epha3/+ due to fully duplicated projections (Figure 4D white and black dots).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 4A,G and inference from map duplication

claim: The median AI value in Isl2Epha3/Epha3 is not significantly different from WT, indicating aligned RC and CC maps.
source: The median AI value (2.20 [2.02; 2.43]) is not significantly different from WT (Figure 4G – Figure 4—source data 1G), indicating aligned RC and CC maps (Figure 4D, black and white dots).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4G and inference from AI values

claim: Median AI values for WT, Isl2Epha3/+ and Isl2Epha3/Epha3 are not significantly different suggesting that RC and CC maps in these animals are aligned, although partially or fully duplicated.
source: Median AI values for WT, Isl2Epha3/+ and Isl2Epha3/Epha3 are not significantly different suggesting that RC and CC maps in these animals are aligned (Figure 4G – Figure 4—source data 1G), although partially or fully duplicated.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4G and inference from AI values

claim: Median values for Isl2Efna3/+ are IDIretino = 5.56 [5.04; 6.07] and IDIcortico = 12.5 [11.8; 13.2].
source: Median values for Isl2Efna3/+ are IDIretino = 5.56 [5.04; 6.07] and IDIcortico = 12.5 [11.8; 13.2] (Figure 4A – Figure 4—source data 1A).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 4A

claim: IDIretino in Isl2Efna3/+ is not significantly different from WT suggesting no dispersion of the RC map.
source: IDIretino is not significantly different from WT suggesting no dispersion of the RC map (Figure 4E, white dots).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and inference from IDI values shown in Figure 4E

claim: IDIcortico in Isl2Efna3/+ is significantly different from WT indicating a spreading of the CC map.
source: However, IDIcortico is significantly different from WT indicating a spreading of the CC map (Figure 4E, black dots).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and inference from IDI values shown in Figure 4E

claim: The median AI value in Isl2Efna3/+ is 4.52 [4.28, 4.76], significantly different from WT, suggesting misalignment between RC and CC maps.
source: This suggests a misalignment between RC and CC maps (Figure 4E) as confirmed by the median AI value in Isl2Efna3/+ (Figure 4G, 4.52 [4.28, 4.76] - Figure 4—source data 1G), significantly different from WT.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4G and inference from AI values

claim: Visual map misalignment is more pronounced in Isl2Efna3/Efna3 (median AI = 8.85 [8.23, 9.26]) compared to Isl2Efna3/+.
source: Visual map misalignment is more pronounced in Isl2Efna3/Efna3 (median AI = 8.85 [8.23, 9.26], Figure 4G – Figure 4—source data 1G) compared to Isl2Efna3/+ as previously shown in vivo (Savier et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 4G and citation to Savier et al., 2017

claim: In Isl2Efna3/Efna3, IDIretino indicates that RC map spreading is similar to WT.
source: Map dispersion value IDIretino in Isl2Efna3/Efna3 indicates that RC map spreading is similar to WT (Figure 4F, white dots; Figure 4A, median IDIretino = 5.56 [5.08, 6.03], not significantly different from WT)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and inference from IDI values shown in Figure 4A,F

claim: In Isl2Efna3/Efna3, IDIcortico indicates dispersion of the CC map (median IDIcortico = 19.1 [17.7, 20.5]).
source: whereas IDIcortico indicates dispersion of the CC map (Figure 4F, black dots; Figure 4A, median IDIcortico = 19.1 [17.7, 20.5] – Figure 4—source data 1A) as demonstrated previously (Savier et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 4A,F and citation to Savier et al., 2017

claim: In WT, Isl2Epha3/+, and Isl2Epha3/Epha3, median local IDVs between RC and CC maps are similar and covary, indicating that the maps are aligned.
source: In WT (Figure 5A), Isl2Epha3/+ (Figure 5B) and Isl2Epha3/Epha3 (Figure 5C), median local IDVs between RC and CC maps are similar and covary (> 0) (WT RC/CC: Jaccard similarity index = 0.60 indicating 60% overlap- covariance = 1.64; Isl2Epha3/+RC/CC: Jaccard similarity index = 0.30, covariance = 88.2; Isl2Epha3/Epha3 RC/CC: Jaccard similarity index = 0.55, covariance = 12.8), indicating that the maps are aligned.
evidence: Supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 5A,B,C and inference from Jaccard similarity and covariance values

claim: In Isl2Efna3/+ and Isl2Efna3/Efna3 animals, median local RC and CC IDVs variation do not superimpose nor covary.
source: This is in sharp contrast to the Isl2Efna3/+ (Figure 5D) and Isl2Efna3/Efna3 (Figure 5E) animals where median local RC and CC IDVs variation do not superimpose nor covary (Isl2Efna3/+RC/CC: Jaccard similarity index = 0.17, covariance = −1.99; Isl2Efna3/Efna3RC/CC: Jaccard similarity index = 0.08, covariance = −4.13).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 5D,E and inference from Jaccard similarity and covariance values

claim: In Isl2Epha3/+ animals, median local IDVretino and median local IDVcortico reach IDVthreshold at 12% and at 8% of the rostral-caudal axis in the SC respectively, consistent with the position of the collapse points.
source: More precisely, in Isl2Epha3/+ animals, median local IDVretino and median local IDVcortico reach IDVthreshold at 12% and at 8% of the rostral-caudal axis in the SC respectively (Figure 5B) consistent with the position of the collapse points described earlier (Brown et al., 2000; Savier et al., 2017 and Figure 3B,D).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 5B and citations to previous work

claim: In Isl2Epha3/Epha3 animals, both RC and CC median local IDV > IDVthreshold along the entire rostral-caudal axis, indicating full RC and CC maps duplication.
source: In Isl2Epha3/Epha3 animals, both RC and CC median local IDV > IDVthreshold along the entire rostral-caudal axis (Figure 5C), indicating full RC and CC maps duplication as shown experimentally (Brown et al., 2000; Triplett et al., 2009; Figure 3F,H).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 5C and citations to experimental work

claim: For both Isl2Efna3/+ and Isl2Efna3/Efna3 CC maps, local IDVs oscillate around the IDVthreshold with a more pronounced effect in the rostral-half of the SC in Isl2Efna3/Efna3 indicating partial duplications of the CC maps.
source: Finally, for both Isl2Efna3/+ and Isl2Efna3/Efna3 CC maps (Figure 5D, dark red, Figure 5E, dark blue, respectively) local IDVs oscillate around the IDVthreshold with a more pronounced effect in the rostral-half of the SC in Isl2Efna3/Efna3 indicating partial duplications of the CC maps in these animals, as demonstrated in vivo (Savier et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 5D,E and citation to Savier et al., 2017

claim: RC median local IDVs in Isl2Efna3/+ and Isl2Efna3/Efna3 animals fall below IDVthreshold indicating single maps.
source: RC median local IDVs in Isl2Efna3/+ and Isl2Efna3/Efna3 animals (Figure 5D pink line, Figure 5E light blue line, respectively) fall below IDVthreshold indicating single maps as demonstrated previously (Savier et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 5D,E and citation to Savier et al., 2017

claim: The 3-step map alignment algorithm is valid and robust in predicting RC and CC maps formation and alignment during development.
source: Taken together, these experimental and theoretical results confirm the validity and robustness of the 3-step map alignment algorithm in predicting RC and CC maps formation and alignment during development.
evidence: Based on inference from the combined experimental and computational results presented in the manuscript

claim: The algorithm generates RC maps for Isl2Epha3/+ heterozygous and Isl2Epha3/Epha3 homozygous animals after 10^7 iterations per run.
source: After 107 iterations per run, the algorithm generates RC maps for Isl2Epha3/+ heterozygous and Isl2Epha3/Epha3 homozygous animals.
evidence: Describes the computational methodology used in the study

claim: In Isl2-Epha3KI animals, the lower RC map corresponds to Isl2(+) Epha3-expressing RGCs, covering 0 to 50% of the rostral-caudal axis in the Isl2Epha3/Epha3 and 0 to 80% of the axis in Isl2Epha3/+.
source: In Isl2-Epha3KI animals, the lower RC map corresponds to Isl2(+) Epha3-expressing RGCs, covering 0 to 50% of the rostral-caudal axis in the Isl2Epha3/Epha3 and 0 to 80% of the axis in Isl2Epha3/+ (Figures 5 and 6 in Brown et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brown et al., 2000

claim: The upper map, corresponding to the Isl2(-) WT RGCs, covers the caudal half (50 to 100%) of the rostral-caudal axis of the SC in Isl2Epha3/Epha3 and 20–100% of the axis in Isl2Epha3/+.
source: The upper map, corresponding to the Isl2(-) WT RGCs, covers the caudal half (50 to 100%) of the rostral-caudal axis of the SC in Isl2Epha3/Epha3 and 20–100% of the axis in Isl2Epha3/+ (Figures 5 and 6 in Brown et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brown et al., 2000

claim: In both Isl2Epha3/Epha3 and Isl2Epha3/+ animals, nasal Isl2(-) RGCs, expressing high levels of Efnas, project to caudal locations in the SC whereas nasal Isl2(+) RGCs, also carrying high levels of Efnas, project ectopically in a more rostral part of the SC.
source: In both contexts, nasal Isl2(-) RGCs, expressing high levels of Efnas, project to caudal locations in the SC whereas nasal Isl2(+) RGCs, also carrying high levels of Efnas, project ectopically in a more rostral part of the SC, where the WT levels of retinal Efnas are normally low (compare Figure 2C with Figure 2I and O; see also Figure 6).
evidence: Based on inference from simulation results shown in Figures 2 and 6

claim: The distribution of RGC projections in the SC in both Isl2Epha3/Epha3 and Isl2Epha3/+ animals leads to a perturbation of the transposed retinal Efna gradients in the SC, generating duplicated Efna gradients along the rostral-caudal axis.
source: Such distribution of RGC projections in the SC in both Isl2Epha3/Epha3 and Isl2Epha3/+ animals leads to a perturbation of the transposed retinal Efna gradients in the SC, generating duplicated Efna gradients along the rostral-caudal axis in both genotypes (Figure 2I,O, Figure 6).
evidence: Based on inference from simulation results shown in Figures 2 and 6

claim: Simulated CC maps are duplicated for both Isl2Epha3/+ and Isl2Epha3/Epha3 and align with the duplicated RC maps as confirmed by in vivo analyses.
source: Consequently, simulated CC maps are also duplicated for both Isl2Epha3/+ and Isl2Epha3/Epha3 and further align with the duplicated RC maps as confirmed by in vivo analyses (Figure 3D,H, Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by simulation results and experimental validation shown in Figures 3 and 6

claim: The ectopic over-expression of Epha3 in the retina has no effect on the expression of Efnas in this structure.
source: Our quantification of Ephas and Efnas throughout the visual system revealed that the ectopic over-expression of Epha3 in the retina has no effect on the expression of Efnas in this structure.
evidence: Supported by experimental qPCR data presented in Figure 1

claim: The redistribution of the molecular cues carried by retinal axons during the formation of a duplicated RC map is sufficient to induce a collicular duplication of the projections coming from V1.
source: Our results suggest an alternative, although complementary mechanism, in which the redistribution of the molecular cues carried by retinal axons during the formation of a duplicated RC map is sufficient to induce a collicular duplication of the projections coming from V1 (Figure 6).
evidence: Based on inference from the combined experimental and computational results

claim: Retinal Efnas, free or bound to Ephas to a limited amount, retain their binding activity in the SC for incoming V1 axons carrying Epha receptors.
source: As mentioned earlier (Savier et al., 2017), in this context retinal Efnas, free or bound to Ephas to a limited amount (Suetterlin and Drescher, 2014), retain their binding activity in the SC for incoming V1 axons carrying Epha receptors.
evidence: Supported by citations to Savier et al., 2017 and Suetterlin and Drescher, 2014

claim: The rearrangement of the retinal Efnas transposed to the SC generates a duplicated gradient which is then encountered by the incoming cortical V1 axons.
